item.title: 何不食肉糜
item.content:encoded:
When told of his starving subjects, Emperor Hui he is reported to have said, "Why don't they eat meat?" The European equivalent is qu'ils mangent de la brioche, let them eat cake. In both cases it is used as an example of wealthy fools out of touch with the realities of life. I've seen it myself: I was once in a room of the great and the good and mentioned the median wage in NZ. After a stunned silence one person looked at another, laughed and said to her "that wouldn't even keep you in shoes!"

In my trade I get to observe the behaviours of what we call High Net Worth Individuals. Most tax authorities have a dedicated team to monitor compliance among this group, because it is fair to say that many of the most aggressive and slippery forms of tax cheating exist among the rich. Keeping an eye on tradies doing a few cashies is important, but the serious leakage occurs elsewhere.

Over the years I've observed some interesting traits around the lifecycle of the rich. As they get wealthier, they have a tendency to isolate from broader society. This allows self-sustaining myths that protect not only their wealth but their egos. It explains how the "shoes" comment above can happen.

Wealth is generally hereditary despite the best efforts of some: the truly self-made-person is rare. Part of this is because it is hard to live without an income while setting out as an entrepreneur. Part is access to capital. And part is simply knowing how the machine works. Bill Gates is a good example: wealthy parents (Bill Gates Snr. who strongly advocates higher taxes for the rich). Imagine how much creativity and natural merit would be released if all clever people were free to realise their potential?

From this foundation, the next stage is to work hard and build something of value in the productive sector - a business that does stuff of value* or makes things. If their parents have connections to the unproductive sector (typically finance or real-estate) then often they go in that direction.

Once the newly rich have built their first pile, it gets secured away. Offshore holding companies, Trusts and so on: all designed to protect that asset so they never need worry about living in poverty, and often to secure a nest egg for their children. Thoughts tend towards intergenerational wealth.

Then they start to realise that being rich only buys so much security. It isn't fun living in a crumbling society. At around fifty years old, many (but by no means all) HNWI's grow a conscience: defining a legacy that make personal values a condition of money - influence from beyond the grave. Theoretically this requires a separation of control in order to work properly, but many find it hard to let go - after all, desire for a legacy can be about ego.

People like Gates and (locally) Tindall are to be congratulated for wanting to give back large chunks of the wealth they were able to acquire by standing on the shoulders of the giants who built our stable society. Gates chooses to do it direct: he has built a non-government administration to distribute cash. By definition this not subject to any democratic controls but there is a lot to be said for bypassing geo-political influences.

Tindall and the other millionaires who asked to be taxed more take a different path: offering more money (tax paid) that can then be allocated through our normal democratic process.

Personally I believe the purpose of an economy is to support people and their environment, but a significant chunk of the population think the opposite: that people exist to support the economy, a model I observe is most enthusiastically supported by those at the top of it. Accepting taxes will not be spent quite how they (I) would have done it can be especially hard for some.**

Ideologies create social division. There is a widely held misconception that right-ish governments tend to manage national finances better than the left. Empirical evidence says there's nothing between them: if anything it points slightly in the other direction. Blinder & Watson is interesting in the current context, and of course Labour bequeathed a war chest to National for the Global Financial Crisis.

It is hard for people (some more than others) to accept that their core beliefs were wrong. I'll put my hand up and admit it took me a while to grasp that a healthy economy is the product of a healthy society, not the other way around; that GDP is a terrible way to measure social progress and that criminalisation of narcotics causes more problems than it solves.

But I think the hardest thing to accept as we get older is that most success and failure is about luck not intellect. That strikes right at the heart of our self worth, and maybe that's the hardest step of all.

-----------------

* Not all services are created equal: one British study shows that for every £1 spent on a tax accountant, about £47 of GDP is destroyed. But every pound spent on a hospital cleaner or childcare worker generates a £10 multiplier. So to enhance productivity employ cleaners not accountants.

** An aspect of this problem is that many people do not grasp where tax dollars go - when people wish to justify tax cheating they tend to focus on headlines. To save you looking it up, here are the top three in NZ. For each $100 you pay in tax about $27 is spent on health, $22 on education and $22 on our universal basic income for those over 65. From the remaining 29%, $1 is spent on housing and community support, $2 on solo parents and $1 on disability support. So if our solo parent support is 10% inefficient, then it's costing you about 10 cents in each $100. If even half our defence spending is a waste (and it isn't), that's $2 down the drain.

item.title: The Veil of Trust
item.content:encoded:
New Zealand has a very high proportion of Trusts per capita: there are many historical reasons for this - tax, hiding assets from the State to receive retirement benefits, protection from creditors, and my personal favourite, controlling children’s lives from beyond the grave*. As things stand today, the vast majority of these trust do noting more than assist with paying the school fees of the lawyers who administer them.

One of the more genuine benefits is privacy, top of the Wikipedia purpose list for a Trust. It is easy to forget that events such as illegitimate children can be a thing, and putting funds in a Trust was an 'honourable' remediation.

But in particular, the wealthy have long sought to reduce visibility of their financial position - it is at the root of why we have tax secrecy. In our society we sometimes come to consider that flashing your cash is vulgar - something that probably arose alongside the concept of wealth itself, and the rich came to realise that the proletariat really do rise up from time to time.

In fact, that’s what tax is - a bargain with the proles in return for not storming mansions and dragging the wealthy into the woods (its a shame that every few generations they have to be reminded).

These concepts run straight into one of the fundamental tenets of Anti-Money-Laundering laws: a prohibition of anonymity. This concept is called out in a pretty stark way in international rules:

FATF recommendation 25.

...in particular, countries should ensure that there is adequate, accurate and timely information on ... trusts, including information on the settlor, trustee and beneficiaries, that can be obtained or accessed in a timely fashion...

This is also the reason that, for the avoidance of doubt, our law contains a specific provision that in the case of Trusts the reporting entity must know source of wealth or funds.

So this creates a tension: it is not the job of a compliance professional to judge the reasoning behind the existence of the Trust.

Communication with the customer is critical - explaining that there is no alternative (despite the various misleading attempts we bump into) but that reporting entities are required to be extremely careful with the information, and only use it for AML purposes.

Taking a lesson from my time at the IRD, culture is a crucial part of defecne. Early in your time at one of my firms you will be called into a room with the Chief Executive for a conversation about respect for peoples lives. Aside from all the legal penalties, people must understand that secrecy is really about decency and values - that is why you don't talk to your friends about what you saw during your work day: not just because you might be punished, but because it is the right thing to do.

But customers should be concerned. All around NZ hundreds of employees of Reporting Entities are collecting and reviewing thousands of documents. This means there is a massive proliferation of copies of identity credentials, bank statements, utility bills and Trust deeds being stored in all sorts of ways - often a folder in a filing cabinet.

The penalties for failing to collect are in reality much higher than those for careless record keeping. That's a problem that needs to be addressed.

* Delightfully known as 'spendthrift clauses'.

item.title: A courageous decision, Minister
item.content:encoded:
Seems I need to post this one about every ten years. IRD recently announced they will be using debt collectors for student loans. There goes the neighbourhood. I’m guessing it was a political instruction, but it will be Peter who ultimately has to clean up the mess.

I suspect the uncollectibles will get handed back to IRD in about a years time, and everyone will shake their heads and wonder who is going to cover the additional costs incurred. Oh yes, that would be us.

I’ve been asked several times over the years why government agencies tend to do their own debt collection. Surely ‘professional’ collectors would be more cost effective?

I was reminded of one of the reasons why not over the last few months as my wife & I have been separately harassed by D&B. Even though they have contacted entirely due to errors on their own part, there has been not a flicker of an apology. In fact they have simply maintained a stance that swings between aggressive and downright rude. If a government department behaved that way, a Minister would lose their job.

It is a courageous agency that outsources this function, because apart from the inefficiency (unless you are small or simply have little internal expertise, outsourcing almost always costs more than the same function performed well internally) the impact is to reduce voluntary compliance. And unlike, say, a retailer owed a debt, government departments do not have the option of simply refusing to do business with their customers again.

Regulatory stance is the term for how you choose to deal with citizens. The agencies goal should be to interfere in lives as little as possible, and if things do go wrong help guide the person concerned back into a state of voluntary compliance.

Repeated errors erode citizen trust. Outsourcing reduces the incentive and opportunity to maintain accurate data. And an aggressive stance simply reinforces the debtors opinion: it allows them to self-justify avoiding the debt.

In the end it will often cost more, erode trust and isolate the agency from a key set of information about their customer, or the policy area being enforced.

item.title: The Next Generation
item.content:encoded:
It’s a pleasure to see that the ‘strines are about to tackle a contradiction in their tax law that we share: treating paid childcare as a personal expenditure. Under NZ law, if you pay for childcare so that you can then go and earn, it’s not regarded as an expense directly related to income.

At this point I should flag that NZ took an alternative path - we pay a subsidy for childcare costs that is a (pretty miserly) means-tested benefit called FamilyBoost. This means it doesn’t disproportionately benefit the wealthy. But it also means that choice is significantly reduced.

If I were an employer and I paid someone to do some of my work so that I had more capacity, that would be called sub-contracting and of course it’s deductible. If I were an MP and parliament provided childcare because the House demands me to work strange hours then it would not be regarded as a fringe benefit.

But pay someone to look after your kids so you can work? That’s fine as they are young and you want to get them out each day, but less so if you would prefer to employ someone to look after them in your own home.

There are obvious historical reasons for this i.e. tradition and conservatism.

In 1970 when the Australian case that cemented the tax rule took place, obviously the little woman should have just gone and found a husband to look after her instead of all this uppity talk of being a lawyer. She could easily have done cleaning or something that would fit in with being a single mum, having had the added advantage of preventing her little brain from overheating.

While rich and powerful have always outsourced their children (including having them wet nursed) our society still has a tendency to frown somewhat at women who don’t want to spend every hour with their offspring. It’s OK for me to say things like “kids are just a pain in the arse” to hearty laughter in the pub, but a woman saying the same thing is likely to meet a less comfortable reaction.

If in 1970 it was largely the very rich who were getting servants to look after their kids, there is possibly an element of class prejudice in the mix.

From a compliance perspective it’s tricky. There is always a concern it will create a chink in the armour. It’s fairly clear that the childcare carveout in our tax laws is sexist and illogical to some extent, but where do you draw the line? Should any servant be deductible? I would argue that childcare is a special case, as it is 7X24 and requires constant attention to be paid. I found it was frowned upon to lock my kids in the bathroom while I went to a meeting.

I think we can define the criteria sufficiently, and put in some caps and ratio’s (should the part of a servants day spent doing housework be deductible too?) But of course that will reduce the tax take. Or will it?

Working parents will do the maths, but I suspect the impact will be less than feared. The childcare worker will pay tax (at a low rate). The employing parent will pay tax at a lower rate than otherwise, but it may increase their gross income and over time this will feed into the economy as higher productivity (reducing the impact of lost years on women’s lifetime earnings). Maybe a bit of a tweak of the thresholds will be enough to offset any change.

It could even have some impact on the systemic underpayment of women compared to men which is at the heart of this governments cowardly (and hypocritical) retreat on pay equity.

Maybe our Minister of Finance will take this on as a balm for the dissonance she must be feeling having just swallowed the frog of abandoning an equity policy she fought so hard for?

item.title: Some fresh veggies with your pork?
item.content:encoded:
Parties erupted in the big tax accounting practices around the country yesterday as Robertson {Labour Minister of Finance} announced possibly the most blatantly batshit election promise: to remove GST from fresh fruit and veg. This should sort out the school fees for a whole generation of tax lawyers, for they will be the great winners.

The disappointment is that it shows a passive approach to fiscal policy that has been a hallmark of the post-social-media era: poll driven policy. Rather than take the time to explain properly (also known as showing leadership) our representatives take the path of least resistance. And especially in this case: mainstream media has been demonstrating a mature and sensible commentary, so there's no excuse.

The bullshit statement that we're "catching up" with other countries is especially insulting. It's a bit like saying we're introducing a fuel subsidy so we can catch-up. Make no mistake - we are regarded as the best in the world, and should this come to pass we will lose that position.

I won't rehash too much why it's stupid, but when even the magnificent Susan St. John from the Child Poverty Action Group is calling it disappointing, you have to wonder what advice these poor buggers are getting.

There are two points that I think have not received the attention they should: the savings shoppers can expect, and why our veggies are so bloody expensive in the first place.

So we take GST off, and stuff gets 15% cheaper right? No. It depends. If the government exempt, then the saving will be about 2.02%. If they zero rate, then we are going to be effectively subsidising the growers and supermarkets through the tax system, because they will be able to claim back the GST on their expenses, without having to pay it on the sales.

Evidence from overseas indicates when it all settles out, prices will drop by about 3-5%. Part of this is because supermarkets will need to shell out a lot of cash to set up their system to cope.

On top of this IRD are going to need a chunk of compliance funding (because when you create a loophole, you have to police it) so this miserly saving (remember it's only fresh fruit and veg) will end up probably costing the rest of us more than it's worth. Oh and don't forget, the people who will benefit the most are the ones who don't need it: it will make Tarquins air-freighted wild strawberries much cheaper. He thanks you.

But why are our prices so high anyway? Land prices (and all the knock-on effects) and lack of competition in the distribution channel (i.e. supermarkets). How does GST at 15% compare to gross profit margin of 70-80%? It's not the growers who make the money.

What should Robertson have announced?

How about simple, easy to administer, well targeted and effective? Child benefit. For the young, every kiwi child used to receive a cash benefit (just like those with a SuperGold card). That's right, a UBI for children. It was paid to parents, and was a flat rate. One interpretation is that this was a tax credit - refunding tax effectively paid by children.

These simple flat taxes are very easy to administer, hard to defraud and tend to get where they need to be. And they don't create gaping holes that will be exploited ad-nauseam.

Now that would really be catching up with the societies we envy.

item.title: Indeed Minister
item.content:encoded:
https://www.artnet.com/artists/gerald-scarfe/yes-prime-minister-red-tape-Y-cxh8JU8tHe1jRPDjvldQ2

Compliance strategy is a subtle profession. We have to balance fairness with administrative efficiency, and in tax that means ensuring that policy is defensible.

New Zealand's toddler government has just applied its first new tax (there will be more to come in order to balance the books) in the form of levying a higher tax on electric vehicles than equivalent petrol cars.

If you ever see a government agency present a media release alongside a political one from the Minister, pay careful attention to the date of any material they reference. With experience you can decode where the Ministry concerned disagrees with the political decision.

In this instance, as an EV owner I received a specific email from the Ministry telling me I would need to buy some km's through the RUC system. So I clicked on the link and eventually was directed to a 2008 report telling me how fair the RUC system was.

That set off alarm bells. 2008? We didn't really have EV's at that time. So, curious, I went to look for the methodology (no link - it needed a Google search... more bells.)

Because I used Google, I also noticed a review that had been done in 2023. It was called a working paper. This is a way for agencies to say what they think when they know the political timing isn't right. It gives weasels (i.e. media relations units) the illusion of an excuse that they don't need to publicise it. I say illusory, because that's not how the Official Information Act works.

It also gives politicians an excuse to say that they hadn't received official advice. Basically room to bullshit.

My point isn't really to highlight what the recent report says. I'm an owner, and will stay an EV user for ethical reasons, and the simple fact I don't like driving archaic victorian technology. EV's are just better in every regard, especially not having to deal with the "loyalty" system rorts that are now prevalent.

But in case you're interested and the report is TLDR, here's a couple of quotes, and a bit of a translation if you don't want to read the whole thing.

"The results in Table 3.3 confirm that current RUC are set higher than the CAM recommendations for heavy vehicles but less than our estimate of the economic cost." {light vehicles subsidise heavy vehicles, and all vehicles have to be subsidised from the general tax pool}

"there is no longer a nexus between money collected from motorists and money spent on roads." {road taxes do not cover road costs - there is no longer a direct link}

And for a normal petrol car, drivers pay $66 per 1000km (in the model) as against an economic cost of $109 per 1000kms (Table ES3). So, petrol cars are subsidised by other vehicles to the tune of about $43 per 1000kms. Have a think about where that subsidy ends up at the end of its journey.

RUC is an administrative pain, but not the end of the world. Nonetheless, a lot of people won't like having a new thing to do. This will cause a compliance issue, but it probably won't be significant. It's a lot harder to disconnect the odometer in a modern car, so I expect the purchase of oversized wheels will increase.

The fairest thing to do would be to remove duty on petrol, but make all cars (irrespective of power train) subject to RUC. This is a not-quite-recommendation that the Ministry have been making for years, and if this government really wants to treat all road users equally, it's probably the answer.

item.title: Tackling the Holidays Act
item.content:encoded:
This is an updated version of a post I first put on LinkedIn. The feedback was positive, so I thought it worth refinement, including some of the ideas that came up.

________________

I have a mate to earns a (good) living cleaning up payroll messes arising from accounting for holidays. In fact I would guess there are hundreds, if not thousands of people employed in the field.

We are not special: this problem is faced all over the post-colonial world. Billions of dollars of pain, not only the cost of fixing it but the businesses who have paid the wrong amount, the employees who didn't notice one way or the other and have either missed out or find themselves in debt. It's a compliance mess.

Our holiday system arises from Christian tradition. Our main holidays are at the wrong time of year and for reasons arising from mythology. So why has nobody grasped the nettle? Political cowardice, and the fear that once a chink appears, the big bad bosses will take advantage.

Of course they will, which is why it is so important to get it right. And that won't happen when it's an overly-complex shitfest.

So here are the beginnings of my prescription.

  1. Abolish all statutory holidays (especially the provincial ones that arise from when the British were thinking administering our country as counties FFS).

  2. Except maybe Waitangi day and ANZAC day (see more below). I think this needs a bit of debate.

  3. Grant an additional 10 days statutory annual leave (i.e. everybody gets a total of 30 days annual leave.)

  4. Establish cultural holiday calendars for through a simple process (administered by the Ministry of Business, Innovation & Employment. The onus is to grant the calendar approval unless it fails to meet specific criteria (e.g. there is already a calendar that is largely similar). These calendars can then accommodate sub-groups of Christianity, Islam etc. or even schooling, sports codes and so on.

  5. The cultural calendars may include Waitangi day and ANZAC day, but they don’t have to.

  6. After employment (casual, part or full time, permanent or otherwise) employees select a calendar that contains 'official' leave days for that denomination. They may choose to select no calendar.

  7. A default, non-denominational calendar is available that includes New Years (2 days - bless the Scots), Matariki, Waitangi and ANZAC days. That’s it.

  8. Nomination may not be requested prior to employment. It cannot be contracted to be a certain calendar, and it can only be changed on anniversary of employment with 28 days notice.

  9. Employers cannot deny leave requests for those official calendar days as selected by the employee. This is so that extended families etc. who rely on days defined well in advance to get together can still do so. Sensible employers will eventually have employees from diverse cultural backgrounds, spreading the holiday load so to speak.

  10. Penalty rules (double pay and a day off in lieu) only apply to employees opting to work on one of their nominated holidays. This is entirely voluntary.

  11. Employers are permitted to mandate up to an additional 5 days per year when leave days must be taken that may vary in addition to the cultural calendar. This is to enable business wide maintenance / quiet period shutdowns etc.

  12. Maintain current practice of the emplyee requesting leave, and the employer making efforts to accomodate within the context of business oeprations.

  13. Prohibit public holiday surcharging, along with all the archaic rules about when businesses must close.

  14. This includes closing rules that apply to Waitangi Day and ANZAC day. We do not force people to vote, fight or pray, so we should not force them to commemorate. This is a bit like the compulsory voting argument.

  15. As a transition mechanism, employers have the right to have current entitlements independently priced, and then pay out any historical obligations over the first two years following introduction.

What have I missed?
